subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-RESPONSIBILITY OF MINISTERS TO ANSWER QUESTIONS RELATED TO PREVIOUSLY HELD PORTFOLIOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning which I gave Your Honour notice earlier this morning. It pertains to the incapacity of members of the House to obtain information from ministers of the Crown on matters which were properly their responsibility when they were ministers of different departments on previous occasions. On Tuesday of this week Your Honour ruled concerning a question put to the present Minister of Regional Economic Expansion on a matter for which he was responsible when minister of transport. Your Honour ruled it was not proper for a minister to provide answers to questions which pertained to his previous responsibilities.
In light of Your Honour's ruling, and in light of further revelations concerning criminal proceedings which have arisen as a result of alleged illegal activities of the Hamilton Harbour Commission, there is very real concern by members on all sides of the House, and the public, with regard to obtaining from the former solicitor general his view of the proceedings alleged to have taken place in the summer of 1972.
A councillor of the city of Hamilton stated that the former solicitor general was given documentary evidence, on the basis of which he should have initiated certain proceedings. It is alleged he did not do so for many months. If Your Honour finds there is a prima facie case of privilege with regard to former ministers providing information which is of concern to members of the House, and for the purpose of clearing the record for their own benefit, I would like to move that this matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections so that the minister in question will have the opportunity to appear before that committee and clarify the situation.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-RESPONSIBILITY OF MINISTERS TO ANSWER QUESTIONS RELATED TO PREVIOUSLY HELD PORTFOLIOS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is an important question of principle. I believe it is in accordance with the traditions of the House and its usages that ministers are cross-examined on their departmental responsibilities. While I recognize that it is a very difficult problem, I feel that unless we adhere to this principle parliament will not be able to fulfil its function as it should.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-RESPONSIBILITY OF MINISTERS TO ANSWER QUESTIONS RELATED TO PREVIOUSLY HELD PORTFOLIOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I admit this is a very difficult problem which has been posed to Your Honour. You must consider a number of factors. For example, the public accounts committee deals with matters which go into the past. If a rule of that kind were adhered to, it would be exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, to obtain the kind of information the committee wished if ministers in charge of departments at the time the items complained of were in the government's responsibility were no longer there.
I refer Your Honour to Standing Order 39. I think we have to commence discussion on the rules with regard to written questions, because the rules for oral questions spring from the rules for written questions. I quote from Standing Order 39:
Questions may be placed on the order paper seeking information from ministers of the Crown relating to public affairs-
I emphasize the words "public affairs": it is not "public affairs limited to the responsibility of the minister of the department concerned". I suggest that when we address questions to ministers of the Crown, we are questioning the ministry as a whole. One minister, because he occupies a certain portfolio, might have specific knowledge of a particular subject matter, but I suggest to Your Honour that until the discussion the other day I doubt whether

Privilege-Mr. Broadbent
there had been a hard and fast ruling on that point; and, of course, the question period itself has been developing over a period of time into its present form.
I submit to Your Honour and to members on the government side that it would be monstrous to permit a minister who had been in charge of a portfolio and who subsequently had been removed from that position to say that because his responsibilities had been changed he could not be questioned as to events which happened during the time he occupied the previous position. Of course, the questions must be related to public affairs, and what we were trying to discuss in the House and in committee are surely public affairs of the greatest magnitude.
It is all very well for one minister to say he will inform himself from another minister; this does not have the same effect as subjecting the minister directly concerned to public scrutiny by way of questions from the opposition or, for that matter, from the government side. If it all has to be done by hearsay, one minister might hide behind the interpretation placed upon a situation by another minister and a great deal of the value of the question period would be lost. I ask Your Honour to consider this matter seriously because your ruling could have an impact on the value of the question period.

subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-RESPONSIBILITY OF MINISTERS TO ANSWER QUESTIONS RELATED TO PREVIOUSLY HELD PORTFOLIOS
speechtext:
I must confess, Mr. Speaker, that I heard your ruling the other day with some astonishment. Certainly, it has never been my impression that a minister could not be questioned about a matter over which he had exercised responsibility. The ruling that a minister could not be questioned about matters for which at one time he was responsible, but for which he is no longer responsible, means that in order to wipe the record clean of anything which may have transpired, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) can simply ask the members of the cabinet to play musical chairs by stepping over one pace to the right; the whole record would be wiped clean, or at least questioning would be prevented. I do not think this was ever the intention of our rules.
Ministers who have been responsible for certain matters ought to be open for questioning about those matters. The situation is analogous to that of a privy councillor; there is a shared and continuing responsibility even for actions taken when a member occupied a portfolio which later was relinquished for another. I respectfully submit that Your Honour might wish to reconsider the effect of your decision.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-RESPONSIBILITY OF MINISTERS TO ANSWER QUESTIONS RELATED TO PREVIOUSLY HELD PORTFOLIOS
speechtext:
Order. I will hear other hon. members- there are several who wish to contribute to the discussion-and I shall certainly give the matter very careful consideration and reserve my decision. There has, however, been comment that some hon. members were caught by surprise or somewhat astonished by my recent decision that ex-ministers ought not to be questioned. Before the discussion proceeds, I think I should refer hon. members who want to participate in the discussion to citation 171 (11) of Beauchesne, found at the top of page 149, which provides that questions ought not to "seek from an ex-minister information with regard to transactions during his term of office". That is as clear and explicit as

it can possibly be, and I have a little difficulty understanding why hon. members are astonished by that.
Furthermore, at page 323 of May's eighteenth edition, under the heading "Questions to unofficial members", under paragraph (u) the following appears:
-and a question to an ex-minister with regard to transactions during his term of office has been ruled out of order.
I put that on the record only to indicate that there is a very clear and explicit foundation that I think would direct us into a situation where questions could be put, on a broader interpretation, to privy councillors who sit on the opposition side of the House in regard to responsibilities that they had at one time when they were in the ministry, and I would have some difficulty with that.
In any case, I want to put the foundation for my decision on the record. What I am troubled about is not so much the very clear citation that relates to use of the question period and the specific responsibilities of ministers during the question period, but I take it that the point raised by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) relates to a much broader context, namely, that there is difficulty, not so much on the question period but in getting information from ministers in other ways before the standing committees; then it would seem to me that any member can be called before a standing committee and asked questions about matters on which he may be able to contribute information that would be of some value in the study of any matter put before the standing committee. If there is some difficulty there, this is a point that I should like to review further, but I did want to put that on the record before hearing other members.

subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-RESPONSIBILITY OF MINISTERS TO ANSWER QUESTIONS RELATED TO PREVIOUSLY HELD PORTFOLIOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the question of privilege raised by my hon. friend, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). Initially, I should like to point out that my friend was very careful not to question the ruling Your Honour made the other day. I may feel, as my leader does, restricted by the nature of that ruling; but I have to say that it seems to be supported by citations in Beauchesne's fourth edition, not only the one to which you referred but also citation 178 which states:
Questions addressed to ministers should relate to the public affairs with which they are officially connected, to proceedings pending in parliament, or to any matter of administration for which the minister is responsible.
The point of the question of privilege is that under the rules as they are, and in light of the precedents, we are stuck with this difficulty of not being able to question a minister concerning a responsibility that is no longer his because he has been moved to some other department. As the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) pointed out, this could pose a real difficulty. If, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) comes back on Monday, he were to move the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) to some other post, then we could not question him on what has been going on, and so on.
It is because of this that the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby would like to see this matter referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections on the basis of a motion under a question of privilege so that in the committee there could be a discussion of how we can cope with this matter. I realize that many questions of privilege do not meet the definition under the rules, but I think the privileges of members of parliament are affected, in the sense that they are trying to get information to which they are entitled but are frustrated by a situation over which at the moment they seem to have no control. I think, therefore, Your Honour's ruling should be that this
Privilege-Mr. Broadbent
matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
In the meantime, we have had the statement of the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) and the suggestion of the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence). I would urge Your Honour not to try to give a ruling today, but to hold this matter in abeyance for a day or two until we see whether ways are found or offered of getting this information. If that is the case, nothing further may need to be done about it. If we are still being frustrated in respect of legitimate right that should obtain for members, then I think Your Honour should find in favour of the proposal made by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby.
I submit that the issue is a terribly important one. No one is suggesting, even by questions, any guilt; but when questions are raised about the conduct of members of parliament or members of the government we owe it to the people of this country to have the matters clarified. We also owe it to the ministers whose names have been mentioned to have the matters clarified. I think, therefore, that the matter is of such importance the Minister of Supply and Services should take the opportunity of pursuing his suggestion of a few moments ago. If that does not meet our needs, then after consideration I submit Your Honour should rule in favour of the question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak for a few moments on the very important principle of whether or not members of this House have a right to require or invite a former minister to appear before the appropriate committee which is dealing with a matter which came under his jurisdiction at some former time when he was a minister of the Crown.
In 1964, when I was not a member of this House, the question arose in the public accounts committee about whether or not there had been impropriety in the letting of a contract to operate the restaurant and bar at the Montreal airport. I had been minister in charge of the department at that time. The public accounts committee decided that, as the minister who six years before had been in charge of the department, I should be asked to appear before the committee to answer questions put to me by the members of the committee.

March 14, 1975
Privilege-Mr. Broadbent
The chairman of the committee at that time, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), contacted me in Montreal and asked me to appear before the committee. I immediately accepted the invitation and came to Ottawa, where I was subjected to very searching questions for a very considerable time before the committee. I might say I was able to demonstrate clearly that there had been no impropriety-

Mr. Speaker, there is one point I should like to make to Your Honour before you consider this matter. Last night I moved a motion in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs to have the former solicitor general, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), called as a witness as a result of a question asked of his successor the present minister. That motion was ruled out of order by the chairman of the committee.
Your Honour has already read the citations with regard to questions asked in the House of ministers in respect of their previous administrative responsibilities, but if we are to be further restricted in standing committees during the examination of the estimates, then we would be denied any opportunity whatsoever to call ministers and question them regarding any of their administrative responsibilities past or present. Therefore, I would ask Your Honour to consider this matter very carefully and review the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs of last night and, more particularly, the ruling of the chairman of that committee.
Finally, may I say that the whole matter could be resolved quickly if the government House leader would stand in his place and have this whole matter referred to a committee, as we have been endeavouring to have done for the past few days.

subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-RESPONSIBILITY OF MINISTERS TO ANSWER QUESTIONS RELATED TO PREVIOUSLY HELD PORTFOLIOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, should like to say a few words. My first words might surprise Your Honour. With respect, I think that the question of privilege of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) is almost out of order in the sense that it is in a vacuum or is hypothetical. Four or five days ago I asked a question about which, obviously, we had all had notice. At that time, because we were in the midst of the question period, I did not really debate the point at issue with Your Honour, although I was interested in the ruling which certainly changed the form of my question.
I think there are two points which have not been mentioned yet. We are discussing this matter in theory, really,

because obviously there are times during the question period when this very point might arise and I would have thought, with respect to all my colleagues, that that would have been the time to debate the point, when Your Honour had before you the actual situation of a question being asked and could see just what the question was trying to get at.
Your Honour said that some of the rules in Beauchesne show quite clearly that the practice is that one cannot ask ministers of previous administrations about past transactions in their departments. There is no question about that so far as I am concerned. However, what is different here-and, again, it depends upon anticipation of questions and I think we know what the questions may be-is that this is not a question about a departmental transaction in terms of policy of the Department of the Solicitor General and why, for example, there was rehabilitation for prisoners under the former minister and not under the new minister. In that way, obviously we would pollute the whole parliamentary process more than it is polluted today.
This matter goes to something not in a departmental way. First, if we had the facts before us in the question period-undoubtedly the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), from the general statement he made, knew that he might be involved in these questions-it would be evident that they did not involve the Solicitor General in terms of how he administered a certain policy of his department with respect to which now, four, five or three years later we are trying to ask questions retroactively.
The minister is a member of the Privy Council and a member of this cabinet and this government. That is a little more relevant than the case of a minister who is no longer around, or the case of an opposition privy councillor who is no longer in the administration. So, first, it is a relevant situation because he is a member of a government. Second, and most important, it is not a question of departmental transactions but a question of credibility, where the minister involved is in the cabinet and is a member of the Privy Council. Surely that must be relevant and it separates this matter, I suggest, from the precedent cited where questions concerned past departmental transactions.
The third matter which really points out why the issue is credibility is that in the evidence given to the committee last night, quite properly the Solicitor General said he had talked to his predecessor who told him certain things. That is hearsay. Since last night many of us have heard a direct contradiction of the hearsay evidence given by the Solicitor General about his predecessor. Obviously, the best way to clear up any conflict in respect of this evidence is to hear direct evidence from the former solicitor general, or direct evidence by the man who is contradicted-in this case, Mr. Campbell.

I just wanted to make a couple of brief points on this matter which has already been discussed so fully. My first point is with reference to citations, which Your Honour has quoted on two occasions, in which the word "ex-minister" is used. It seems to me that it is possible to interpret that word a little more broadly than one might suspect. Ex-minister may not necessarily mean a minister who was formerly responsible for a department and is now responsible for another department. He is still in fact a minister, not an ex-minister. Ex-minister may mean someone who is no longer a minister at all.
The second point I want to make is that the practice in this area has not been as clear cut as some people might suggest. May I say with the greatest respect to you, Sir, that I have before me a copy of Hansard containing a question and answer which you have allowed concerning a matter which had been the responsibility of a minister at an earlier time. I should like to refer you to page 2879 of Hansard for February 4, at which time a question was put to the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) concerning an event which occurred while he was minister of national health and welfare.
I will read the question and answer, which deal with arsenic pollution in Yellowknife. The following is the question put to the Minister of Labour:
Having been the minister responsible for health at the time this report was initially produced and tabled, could he explain why the health study was not initiated at that time?
The question was allowed, and the minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot recall at the moment, but I could check into it with my colleague.
This is an example, it seems to me, of this procedure being allowed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-RESPONSIBILITY OF MINISTERS TO ANSWER QUESTIONS RELATED TO PREVIOUSLY HELD PORTFOLIOS
speechtext:
Order, please. As indicated earlier, this is a matter which I think deserves the most careful consideration. I think there are a number of areas that are quite clear. I take it that the citations in Beauchesne make it quite clear where the responsibility lies during the question period itself. There are both precedents for prohibitions or disallowance of questions put to ministers about their former responsibilities and admonitions that questions should be directed to ministers about their current responsibilities. I think that fact remains strong and clear.
However, I feel in addition that the chair does not have the power ever to prevent a minister from answering a question which he wishes to answer. It is one thing to suggest that, if a minister raises an objection on technical grounds to answering the question, the question must be examined to see whether the technical grounds are correct. However, if a question is put and the minister wishes to answer it, I am sure it would be improper for the chair to try to stop him from doing so.
In addition, suggestions have been made that the chair review the procedures of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. Whatever the dimensions of the problem may be, it is also abundantly clear that the chair does not sit on appeals to procedures in standing committees. These committees are masters of their own procedures.

subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-RESPONSIBILITY OF MINISTERS TO ANSWER QUESTIONS RELATED TO PREVIOUSLY HELD PORTFOLIOS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-RESPONSIBILITY OF MINISTERS TO ANSWER QUESTIONS RELATED TO PREVIOUSLY HELD PORTFOLIOS
speechtext:
I should say that the corollary of the committees being masters of their own procedures is that the committees have very wide powers, provided they are in agreement to take a certain step. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), once the committee agreed to invite him, there was no problem with his being there. There may be difficulty with the committee coming to such an agreement, but in that case it is not a matter with which the chair should concern itself.
In the final analysis, I again see the question of privilege of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broad-bent) as touching not simply the narrow question about the question period, but also the wider question as to whether hon. members' privileges are restricted because they are stopped, not only by the rules in the question period but by other procedures, from having access to information which they feel they have a right to obtain. That is the wider question which I propose to review and upon which I shall reserve my decision, not only in the hope that the arguments provided will throw some light on the question but also because possibly, with the passage of two or three days, there may be some agreement among members of the House to try to resolve this question on their own volition.

speechtext:
I rise this afternoon to make a few comments on matters that I think have not until now been mentioned and which should perhaps be brought to the attention of the minister and the country. In the last several months following the throne speech debate the minister has indicated that a steady stream of agricultural legislation would be presented. There appeared, to everyone who read the press, to be a long list of measures that were apparently intended to open up a new era so far as agriculture is concerned. I think that anyone who perhaps did not give this matter very serious consideration, keeping in mind the complications and implications of all these legislative items, might in fact get that impression.
The minister has travelled throughout the country reciting one item of legislation after another which will come before the House. In fact, some of these items are now before the House. What the minister does not tell the people and the country is that in none of these items of legislation is there an inkling or a suspicion of new areas being opened up in so far as agriculture is concerned: the minister is merely introducing amendments. Certain amendments may be necessary to update the legislation, but it is not acceptable to the agricultural community in this day and age to have to depend on legislation enacted at some period of time in the past to cover specific situations which do not necessarily exist today. The fact that the minister's proposals contain nothing more than amendments to existing legislation indicates that this government has no new ideas of its own.
I find that most of the legislative items dealing with farm credit, stabilization and other matters pertaining to agriculture relate to ideas introduced at the time the Conservative Party was in office. I am not suggesting there is anything wrong with the legislation; the legislation is good, and certain amendments are necessary. It is totally incomprehensible that this minister should roam around the country making one speech after another without putting forth any new idea of his own. He certainly

March 14, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
has enough people writing speeches for him as it seems he is delivering, on average, about two speeches a day: they are coming fast and furious from all sides.
I have been hoping, in vain, that the minister would take a new approach. I find it almost disgusting that the minister should always refer back to the original piece of legislation. The preamble to the original bill, for example, recognized the increase in the cost of production as compared to the income received by farmers. The minister simply rearranges the preamble and puts it into the new bill, then refers to it as a great, new innovation or new approach to agriculture. Then each one of his trained seals gets up one after the other and praises the minister to high heaven.
I really wonder why we must spend time debating this bill, because when looking at the past performance of the government under this legislation it is obvious that the minister could have done almost anything he wanted. This legislation already gives him the authority to support agricultural products. The minister shakes his head, indicating that he cannot. Let me suggest again to the minister that he could have done anything he wanted; he could have supported any item he felt required support, under the provisions of this act as it now stands.
It is true that there are certain commodities in respect of which there is mandatory support. I have before me an annual report which lists about 28 commodities that have been supported in the 16 years since this act was enacted. This indicates that the minister did have the authority to support any agricultural commodity he wished to support. The minister has supported various commodities in the past by order in council. As a result of research, I have found that the minister not only can support whatever items he wants but he can support them at whatever level he wishes.
The minister makes a lot of noise about the fact that with the new amendments it will be possible to support the mandatory commodities on a five-year average rather than a ten-year average, and that the new level of support will be 90 per cent rather than 80 per cent. For the information of the House, there are many items which have been supported in the past at a level higher than 80 per cent. I would ask the minister to indicate to the House the present level of support in respect of cattle. I can tell the House that at the present time the minister obviously has the authority, because support is at the level of 154 per cent on the ten-year average. No new ground is being broken by these amendments; the minister has the authority to support these commodities at any level.
Let me go through this list very quickly to indicate some of the items and the levels at which they have been supported in the past. In the year 1971-72 hogs were supported at 88.5 per cent; in 1971 sugar beets were supported at 117 per cent, blueberries at 105.5 per cent, rutabagas at 83.3 per cent, and carrots at 93.4 per cent. Further on in the list we find that in 1972-73 apples were supported at 90.3 per cent, and fowl at 251 per cent. What new ground is being broken? Let us consider the other side of the coin. In 1973, for example, the support in respect of potatoes was at the 78.1 per cent level. In other words, the minister could have supported any item above or below the 80 per cent level except for those mandatory items.

Without the provision of additional funds, what additional safeguards will the farmers have as a result of these amendments? I suggest that what the minister is telling the farmers around the country about the results of these amendments is just a lot of boloney. This minister has the authority to support these commodities, but he is doing nothing. He is telling everyone that the farmers must get more, but he does nothing about it himself. The potato producers are at this moment crying to the minister to do something. He does not require additional authorization, he can act under the existing legislation. Potatoes have been supported in the past and there is nothing preventing the minister from introducing support again at this time. All that is required is a few minutes in cabinet to convince the minister's colleagues. That is what he should be doing, instead of running around the country talking to all the farmers but doing nothing.
If one looks at the record of the minister's speech, he will see that the minister is actually preparing the farmers for a drop in income this coming year. He is paving the way by telling the farmers that they will have to accept a reduction in income. He tells us here that he has a formula to take into account the cost of farm production, but there is nothing that would prevent him from supporting potato prices under the existing legislation, for example. The minister can support any commodity that requires support in order to increase the farmers' income. He is not doing it; he is running around telling everybody that their prices are too high and that the farmers need more money, yet he will not do anything about it.
He has legislation in effect today to do this. The minister can run around telling everybody that legislation is being introduced, but now is the time to act. He makes speeches in which he threatens one group or another. Obviously he cannot do anything about the cost of production, but he can do something about the income of the producers. The minister has the legislation but is not acting on it. Now he says he needs more. This is all window-dressing which makes it possible for the minister and all his supporters to write letters and have every newspaper in the country, every week, write columns in which it is suggested that amendments have been introduced to the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Then everybody sits and waits in expectation.
What happens? The farm incomes will go down about 15 per cent. The minister says he will guarantee a certain cost of production and that he will set it at 90 per cent. At best this is a backward process. It is to be set at 90 per cent of what the producers have had in the last five years. The fact is that cattle are supported at 154 per cent at this moment, and farmers find this insufficient for their needs today. We might take a look at the cattle industry. The minister did not have to stop at even 154 per cent. The farmers' unions have been asking for a support price of $65 per hundred, while at this moment I believe it is $45.42 per hundred. The minister has one thing stuck in his head.

Yes, he has egg all over his face. The minister represents restricted production. The minister has told us that he will take into account the increase in the cost of production and other needs. I might mention some of the things we see when we pick up the newspapers. I will give one example. I see that the posties are demanding a 71 per cent basic salary hike. Their present salary is $4.59 an hour and they are asking for an additional $3.26 per hour, which will bring their salary up to almost $8 per hour. A salary of $8 per hour, calculated on a weekly basis, represents almost $300 a week.
Without arguing the pros and cons of the demands of these workers, may I say that these people come in at an appointed hour, do a certain amount of work and no doubt have a coffee break and a warm place waiting for them. No doubt a cafeteria is provided for them so they may have their lunch, and so on. I have seen some of these things around the departments, and it seems that they are ready to leave about 15 minutes before quitting time. Like horses at the starting gate, they wait for the bell to ring and are off to catch a bus. That is as far as their responsibility goes.
I wonder how many people would like to receive $300 for a steer. If one had 50 steers a year, this would represent $15,000, equal to the posties. This does not necessarily mean that that would be clear money, because not only must the producers pay for the feed but they also have their capital investment, the land, the interest and the input costs. The producer must consider all these things before he can think about the same amount received by one worker. This amount of $15,000 would equal the sale of 50 steers.
If this minister were realistic and realized what is going on around him today, and if people such as the posties have the right to make such demands, then the minister has the right to ask the same for the farmers. His responsibility does not end just by making a speech. He must do something with the legislation he has before him, and he has not done so. There is no indication that he intends to do this. This is what is so frustrating to us. The minister could have been doing something, but instead he stands up and says that rather than a ten-year average there will be a five-year average, and the guarantee will be 90 per cent.
Why must the minister stop at 90 per cent? What is wrong with 100 per cent? This still would not be enough: with the addition of the cost of production, it would only be a break even point. What is the minister's explanation for setting the support at the level it is? It is not intended that the producers make a profit; this is a "stop loss" program. I wonder how people like this when it comes from the Minister of Agriculture who is touted around the country as being a friend of the farmer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before lunch I was saying that the minister had travelled through this country leaving the impression with the press and with all those who cared to listen to him that he was introducing updated legislation, and that it was necessary for the survival of the farming industry. In fact, he even left the impression that this would improve the business of farming. However, I was able to point out in the course of my remarks that the minister already had the necessary legislation which was passed by a Conservative government, and he did not have to run around the country making speeches and suggesting that further legislation was necessary. What he does not have is the will to work for the people, and will cannot be legislated. It will be up to him and his colleagues in the cabinet to produce that will. If there's a will, there's a way, as has been pointed out to the government frequently in the last 16 years since this legislation was first introduced.
Let me illustrate a point with regard to the stabilization of the price of certain commodities, for example, certain grades of cattle. Under the present bill the government has extended the stabilization program for the first time in 16 years. When one looks at the annual report, one finds that it contains no mention of cattle; but for the first time in 16 years the government is proposing to stabilize the prices of cattle, specifically of grades A, B and C. Of course, those are not the only grades of cattle. The minister must realize that if we are to assist farmers, we must provide them with sufficient income to enable them to stay in farming. However, obviously the minister will not do it because he does not have the will. Another approach must be adopted.
I should like to go on to another matter. The other day the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) asked the minister about the possibility of a stabilization price for honey. It may interest this House to know that not only do we produce grain and a lot of cattle in the area I come from, but we also produce honey. There is a need for stability in that product. The minister wanted to know what kind of a system there was for marketing honey, and that implied to me that the only way producers will get stability is to go to a marketing board. That is the only purpose the minister has in mind, I believe; but he does

March 14, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
not need a marketing board in order to provide stability. There is no marketing board for cattle and he can provide stability there, so he does not need one for honey.
Several years ago a subsidy was provided for wool, but then it was dropped. It had amounted to something like $12 million. My information is that the subsidy was dropped because production was not increasing sufficiently. That would appear to mean that perhaps the subsidy was not high enough to entice producers. It seems that in the last few years all the problems of agriculture have been solved by gradually cutting down the number of producers and the amount of production to the point where we have to import commodities.
It is amazing that a country that is so forward looking in other ways should be so backward in its thinking in this regard. It seems there is a stigma attached to agriculture. If you speak on behalf of agriculture, you are not supposed to know anything else; this is the prevailing attitude. It does not matter what kind of background you come from, if you are associated with an occupation other than agriculture you are on a higher level. As a result of depressed prices we are losing farmers every day and a strange parallel is developing. Just about a year ago we were told we had ample supplies of natural gas: we had oil to burn, so to speak; we were able to export it and did not have to pay any attention to fuel consumption in automobiles, and so on. Then suddenly there was a great shortage and we started scrambling in the other direction.
We now find ourselves in the same situation with regard to agriculture. I think we should treat the farmers as well as anybody else. The posties have demanded a 71 per cent increase in salary, which would bring them to something like $8 an hour. Surely we should pay the farmer an adequate price for his commodity and encourage him to stay on the land. Farmers do not want a guaranteed income just to sit around and do nothing, and I am not suggesting this; but I am in favour of paying them enough for their products so they will see the advantage of staying in production. Farmers can take their ups and downs. The annual report for 1973-74 published by the Agricultural Stabilization Board shows that $1,459 million was spent to stabilize the prices of commodities during the 16 years to 1974. Of this amount, $875 million was transferred to the Dairy Commission, $92 million was for hogs and $154 million was for milk. Indeed, if you take away all the dairy aspect of the subsidies, only about $300 million was spent in subsidies for other agricultural products in that 16-year period. Mr. Speaker, this is not sufficient to keep farmers in production.
Farmers have accepted quotas for the production of wheat for human consumption; indeed, they have been asking for it for years. This shows that they are willing to accept quotas, but they want a good price for the commodity. We should gear our production policies beyond our domestic requirements, however, to the extent of 10 per cent or 15 per cent to provide protection against the difficulties of nature and other circumstances over which we have no control.
The world will always demand food and as taxpayers, not as individual producers, we should willingly donate any surplus to the hungry people of the world. If we can obtain agreements in this respect with other countries,
[Mr. Korchinski.l
that is fine, but if not we should do it alone. If necessary, we should build storage facilities so that when the time comes these commodities will be available to others. A shipment of grain destined for Pakistan, where people are starving, cannot leave the country because of a stupid shipping tie-up. When we have to work under a threat with a gun at our head, so to speak, it is time that we had storage elsewhere. We have a moral obligation to the rest of the world. We have the capacity, the ability and the know-how to produce grain and many other commodities, but we have only diverted $300 million in 16 years, roughly $20 million a year, to encourage production.
' We are not doing a lot for agriculture. The minister reminds me of a puff-ball. Anybody who has walked around on the prairies knows what a puff-ball is. It is big, but if you step on it there is a cloud of dust and then nothing. With this minister you might expect something solid in legislation, but when you test it, there is nothing there. If the government were to say, "We will base support prices on other prices prevailing in society, plus 10 per cent," we could go along with it; I do not think farmers would argue with the minister. But he wants to base support prices on the average prices of the last five years. Mr. Speaker, nobody wants to work for last year's salary. Why should agriculture be forced to produce for prices that could be as much as five years old?
What is wrong with the minister? He is like a car with only a reverse gear. It is time he looked forward. Farmers must be enabled to produce enough income to support themselves, otherwise they will go out of business. We do not need the sort of "stop loss" program the minister introduced for cattlemen. How can he protect them adequately with such a program? It is not enough. As it is, cattlemen are not earning enough and the minister's program will only prevent great losses. I do not see how it will enable cattlemen to survive. That is why I say the minister's policies are backward-looking. Why, even now some people are demanding 71 per cent more salary than they were paid last year.
I find that the price guarantees in this bill are totally unacceptable. When you consider the minister's record you will not be reassured that farmers of western Canada or of other parts of the country will be induced to stay in agriculture. With farmers leaving the farm our situation will become difficult. I think that cattlemen have already touched bottom, so to speak. The minister can manipulate the price structure any way he wishes; he can base it on quarterly figures, yearly figures, or any way he wishes- but what good does that do if he will not act? I wish the minister would take into account increases in production costs when considering support levels. He might take some flack from consumers, and Mrs. Plumptre might make a nasty speech about him, but he would be doing the right thing. It is no good saying what must be done and then doing nothing. The minister could do the right thing; he has the means but not the will.
The government, with its majority, will force this bill through, but its approach to the establishment of marketing boards is faulty. The minister comes from an area which produces considerable quantities of milk. I know milk producers face difficulties, but they are not the only
March 14, 1975

ones. If we can spend large sums of money on the dairy industry without being hurt by taxpayer flack, I suggest we can spend similar sums on other areas of agriculture. The national interest demands the support of agriculture. After all, amounts spent on agricultural support will not be overly significant, given total government expenditures which, with supplementary estimates, will approach the $30 billion mark this year.
Frankly, I do not think we need this bill. It does not give the minister powers he did not previously possess. Subparagraph 1.1 of clause 5(2) on page 4 of the bill reads:
For the purpose of stabilizing the price of an agricultural commodity, the board may exercise such other powers as are prescribed by the governor in council for that purpose.
In other words, it does not really matter what the board says, as the decision depends on the cabinet. An order in council must be passed. Mr. Speaker, the old bill contained the same provision; an order in council was necessary. If the minister wants to save the agricultural industry, he will need to act on sound advice. It is clear that in the next year or so there will be a shortage of cattle, primarily because cattlemen cannot survive at present-day prices. The industry will only survive if it is told, under some sort of program, that Canada will require such and such an amount of meat in the next given period and if the price paid for the meat is fair and bears some relation to cost of production. Never mind "stop loss" programs. Don't look back. I ask the minister to look forward, otherwise the situation in agriculture will be comparable to the situation in our petroleum industry. Already we are being told about petroleum shortages.
As the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone) pointed out clearly and ably, our farmers will only produce the food needed for feeding our population and the starving peoples of the world if conditions are right and if they are induced to stay in food production. If conditions are not right, they will leave the business of farming and we shall all lose. This bill is not adequate. The minister is looking back. Only if he turns round and looks forward will he provide the stability for agriculture which is necessary if the industry is to survive.
I do not think I need say any more except this: I hope that one year from now we shall not find that the agricultural producer's income has declined and that the minister has done nothing to help him. So far he has not demonstrated that he truly wants to do anything. Mr. Speaker, it is not a change in legislation that we need; it is a change in attitude.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall make a few brief comments on Bill C-50, the agricultural stabilization bill. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchin-ski) covered many of the things I wanted to say. His comments about the public profile of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) were particularly apt. I will not dwell on the lack of action in implementing satisfactory agricultural policies. We on my side of the House will in all probability support this bill, but we do not underestimate the dangers inherent in this type of legislation. I am troubled by that part of the bill dealing with support prices across Canada for a commodity. Clause 1(4) on page 2 of the bill reads in part:
Agricultural Stabilization Act
The powers ... conferred by this act may be exercised in relation to an agricultural commodity throughout Canada or in any region in Canada when, in the opinion of the governor in council, the market situation for the agricultural commodity in that region is substantially different from the market situation therefor in the rest of Canada.
The bill will assure that the regionalization of support prices will be recognized, but the cabinet is to make this decision. It can be assumed that in any democratic country like Canada, intervention by the federal cabinet will be based on a political decision taken at a given time. Quite possibly, the decision would be based on political expediency and the desire of the party in power to retain power. This is certainly an area that we on this side of the House would like to see changed for the good of agriculture. When the bill is passed, farmers of that particular commodity from that region of the country who want a specific amount of money will, because of low prices, have to lobby with the government. A lot of valuable time will be lost; the minister's time will be taken up with the various lobbies that must take place because the decision will not necessarily be set down but will be a political judgment by the cabinet of the day.
I wish to raise a point that does not necessarily pertain to the bill. The support price is available for all commodities, as I mentioned before, only in certain regions of the country. This brings me to the point that is starting to be of major concern to many Canadian farmers and farm organizations. Three provinces have already moved toward what has been called a guaranteed income. British Columbia is into this to a certain degree. According to press reports, Ontario is looking at it, and Quebec is certainly looking at it. At the present time there is talk of drafting legislation to be brought forward within the next few months.
When we talk in terms of a guaranteed income we must realize that this will come about in various forms; it will not be standard across the country. Programs would not necessarily be criticized to the extent they are if they were not always tied to production controls. I have not seen all the programs and I have not talked in detail to the ministers involved in drafting the programs; however, it certainly appears as though the guaranteed income approach will be attained through controlling supply and production allocating quotas, and so on. I come from a part of the country which produces more than its people consume. I refer to western Canada. This whole approach could ultimately eliminate the kind of exporting western Canada must do if we are going to maintain a viable agricultural base.
I hope the Minister of Agriculture is looking at the problem. It is of grave concern in various regions of the country. Farmers feel they could not operate under this kind of guaranteed income approach. If this were carried to its logical conclusion, there could in effect be ten so-called guaranteed income programs, one in every province, if in fact the provinces wanted that and if the population or tax base were there to warrant that kind of expense. If that happened, Canada could conceivably be divided into ten regions. In that event it would be very difficult to move products from one area to another

March 14, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
because of the controls involved, our borders and the balkanization that would take place within this country.
If we are going to have any kind of guaranteed income, and I suppose it could be justified for certain commodities, I firmly believe the base for that kind of approach must be established by the federal government. With this legislation, one of the provinces I mentioned previously could supplement the federal money and use it to help run its own guaranteed income program. With the kind of land base and people base we have in this country, I do not know whether Canada is ready for that kind of agricultural program.
I am certainly not an expert on the guaranteed income approach as far as the Quebec situation is concerned. While it may be commendable for some commodities produced in that province, it appears to almost be a European Common Market approach to agricultural problems, whereby you become involved in price support to a very high degree over a period of time, and it disrupts normal market functions. I would not want to see Canada become involved in that to any great extent. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will give consideration to the concerns that have been echoed in this debate and across the country. The minister has discussed the matter with people in various parts of Canada. If the provinces each go their own way for the good of the province, this could have a devastating effect on agriculture in the future.
Talking now about stabilization and the bill itself, the minister will hear one criticism when he brings the bill to committee. Farm input costs have increased tremendously. The price of everything a farmer has to purchase to grow a crop or feed his animals has increased so rapidly that 90 per cent of the five-year average may not be adequate. Because of the present inflationary cycle it may have no significance. This should have been done in the mid-sixties when there was a much lower rate of inflation; price increases did not occur on an almost monthly basis. Looking at the past five-year average, it might have worked; however, I frankly do not think it will have any bearing on the present long-range future of the commodities affected.
When we get to the clause by clause study of the bill I hope the committee will consider this question in total and come up with an amendment to meet the present economic situation. The cost-price squeeze which farmers experienced in the years 1969-71, and from which we moved away to some extent during 1973 and 1974, is back with us again. Farmers have not yet realized the extent of the squeeze which is likely to be forthcoming. In the last few weeks there has been a drastic decline in the prices of most agricultural products. Blame for this cannot be placed on any one government; it is a consequence of general instability in the economy and I cannot see us moving away from this situation for some time. The farmer-businessman who is keenly aware of his costs, and who knows what he must do in order to keep pace with them, is the farmer who will survive what I think is likely to be an extremely difficult period in the next year or two.
There will be opportunities to give the bill further scrutiny in the standing committee. I should like to see
[Mr. Murta.l
committee members sit down with some of the officials and try to agree on an amendment which implies less attention being paid to cost averages when fixing floor prices. Remember, the situation today is different from what it was even two or three years ago and, as I have suggested, the biggest factor has been the rate at which costs have increased. The bill will pass whether the committee does this or not, but unless it is amended it will not prove to be of any real help to the people it is intended to help. I therefore hope that all members of the committee will work toward an amendment of the kind I have outlined. Such a change is needed, and in the future I think it will be desperately needed by farmers in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this bill before it goes to committee. I support the bill. I think we have to recognize that it attempts in some way to provide a reasonable support price for specific agricultural commodities. Of course, such legislation is in no way a substitute for an aggressive marketing policy, something we badly need. We have shown that we are efficient producers, yet in the last five years we have become a net importer of agricultural products. Thus, one of the main priorities-and I am sure the minister shares this point of view-must be to work out effective marketing programs rather than speak about production control and supply management.
Producers want to produce. They do not want to be bound by quotas and regulations. They do not want an agriculture policy which causes them to look inward but, rather, a policy which will create a desire to produce in abundance. I confess I find some contradiction in government policy in this area. We hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) telling farmers to produce to beat the band, and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) says the same thing. At the same time, we hear the Minister of Agriculture talking about supply management. I find it difficult to reconcile these two points of view. When you have asked farmers to produce to beat the band it is difficult to expect them to take kindly to the imposition of quotas and restrictions.
The egg marketing board attempted to control production, albeit ineffectively. What we saw as a result of the efforts made by CEMA was the greater concentration of production in the hands of relatively few people. Two provinces in particular took advantage of the situation and overproduced, as did a number of individuals. Unless we are prepared to place policemen on duty in every egg-grading station, it will be impossible to supervise a supply management program effectively. I do not think agriculture is ready for restrictions of this kind.
Then, again, as members who sat on the committee inquiring into CEMA know very well, it is impossible to administer a program of supply management in the absence of control over importations of the product concerned. I may be wrong, but I believe that among the conditions under which the provinces agreed to become parties to the national egg marketing plan was a stipulation that there should be effective import control; in other words, the imported eggs would be considered on the same basis as though they were supplied by another producer, otherwise there is no possibility of getting a supply management program to work effectively. According to a
March 14, 1975

Canadian Press report quoted by a Prince Albert newspaper, a member of the executive of the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency said on Friday that the agency-
-is having serious internal problems and will either succeed or fail during the next month.
Harold Crossman, one of three executive members on the agency, says the oversupply of eggs in Canada has led CEMA to ask Ontario and Quebec to reduce the number of their laying hens.
Mr. Crossman said he is not optimistic about the agency's future.
He said Quebec would have to make reductions of about 11 per cent and Ontario about 9 per cent.
That agreement was entered into supposedly in good faith, yet we have a situation where the producers and the provinces failed to uphold their terms of the bargain. Indeed, the federal government failed to uphold its terms of the bargain in that it failed to control in any effective way the importation of eggs. The operations of the national egg marketing agency can only be described as nothing less than shameful and wasteful. After all, this is the reason we lost 28 million eggs. Certainly at this juncture it does not augur well for Canadians to be party to a situation where we have people in this world starving and anxious to get their hands on this kind of food, yet we waste it carelessly.
In my opinion, the federal government has not provided a fair climate for giving Canada's agricultural producers confidence in the economy. The producers of this country are entitled to a fair return so as to cover their cost of farm input, production, management and labour. Certainly that is a worthy goal. I realize this bill goes part way in an attempt to achieve that goal, but in my opinion many of the things done by the federal government over the last two years have not necessarily worked toward providing the right kind of climate. As a matter of fact, there have been a number of irritating measures put forward by the federal government. For example, there have been a number of ad hoc, piecemeal attempts to correct industry that is in trouble, but these have met progressively with failure. Since the Minister of Agriculture assumed his portfolio there have been in the order of 29 variations of policy in the beef industry. Another way in which the government has failed to produce a climate that is conducive to a strong agricultural industry is in its failure to deal with inflation. Input costs over the last two years have increased appallingly. I should like to refer to a Free Press report on farming for November 16, 1974. This report gives a pretty good outline of the way in which input costs have risen over the last five years. For example, 11-48-0 fertilizer cost $103 per ton in 1970; this year the projected cost is $200. Weed spray, 2,4-D Ester, five-gallon pails, in 1970 cost $24.95 and the projected cost in 1975 is $70.
Carbyne in 1970 cost $59.90 for a four gallon pail, and the projected 1975 price for that same pail is $75. Avadex was $78 for a pail in 1970 and the projected 1975 price for that same pail is $92. I could go on to tractors, diesel fuel and what not, but the point is that most of these things are manufactured in this country. We hear the argument that our inflation is imported from abroad, but that certainly does not hold true in respect of these products which are manufactured here.
The over-all approach of the government is that we must learn to live with inflation. I suggest the government by its policies is fanning the fires of inflation, and this has caused a great deal of the difficulty in the agricultural production sector of our economy. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) talked about past averages. If the government does not adopt an effective anti-inflationary policy these past averages will not work to the benefit of the farmer. This policy of failure on the part of the government does not only perpetuate these difficulties in respect of the producers but also in respect of the consumers and everybody else.
The government has also failed to deal effectively with strikes. All we see in newspaper headlines today are references to strikes in various parts of the country. The Ottawa Citizen of Friday, March 7, carried the heading "Govt, should end strikes: wheat pool official". The only thing that will help them is strong decisive leadership from that group over there. The Minister of Agriculture sits there very smugly, and suggests that we must let the collective bargaining process take its course. I suggest that when 300 or 400 grain weighers and samplers can tie up a multi-million dollar industry it is absolutely shameful. The minister cannot take consolation in the fact that his colleagues say we must not interfere with the collective bargaining process. Surely the public interest is more important at this stage of the game than the interests of these few hundred people. The government could act, but it has failed to do so.
The minister can boast very boldly about this piece of legislation. I am not denying him credit for introducing this bill, but is he prepared to recommend to his government that the producers who are being severely affected by these strikes should be given some protection or some insulation? They paid the $17 million demurrage bill last year. That was a total waste of money, but nothing compared to the loss of something in the order of $200 million to $300 million in income to the farmers. This loss is being incurred because of our forward sales agreements which establish the price of grain at the time of delivery. There has been relatively no grain shipped for the last month, and prices have tumbled in the last 60 days by as much as $1 to $1.50 a bushel. In spite of that this minister, who contends to be the champion of the farmer, will not put pressure on his cabinet colleagues to move to help those farmers immediately, and not on the basis of a five year average.
The solutions are not simple, but they require some guts and some leadership. Transportation is another area directly related to the income capability of producers. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board talks about abandoning Crowsnest pass freight rates, and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) says we are not going to touch those rates. This creates confusion, apprehension, and frustration in the minds of producers in western Canada. It seems that, if we do not have a strike that slows down the movement of grain, we have a transportation failure.
The philosophy of the government is to use a lot of words, mouth a lot of expressions, but when the chips are down it fails to come through with any meaningful actions or programs of assistance.

I see nothing wrong with departments that are concerned about trade and all these other things working together and coming to a mutual understanding on what we are trying to do about food production in this country. I have been accused of being just a representative of the farmers. That is a damn lie, and I will say so at mass on Sunday if anybody wants me to do that. They lost 1 per cent of total production, and they did not even know where the chickens were laying them. How can you condemn them for that?
You could look at the automobile industry in my area. The hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) did not say a damn thing about that the other day. The highest priced computers you can buy, the highest priced market analysts you can hire, the highest priced marketing forecasters you can get all made horrendous mistakes in the automobile industry. They did not know what happened. People quit buying cars. All computers told them was that production should continue, but did you see a request for an inquiry into that?
We know that losses in automobile production have cost this country 1,400 times the amount we lost when eggs went bad. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that some of the experts on whose predictions automobile production is based earn more than the Prime Minister. We do not say that the difficulties in automobile production were the result of stupid marketing policies. If unemployment rises by 4 per cent in any district, the entire nation pays the bill for unemployment insurance. In my area unemployment is at the 10 per cent level because of the horrendous mistakes made by some high-priced market computer specialists. Do people say that the workers are at fault in this situation, or that marketing and computer specialists were wrong? Why blame the difficulties in egg production on agricultural producers?
Agricultural Stabilization Act
I was surprised to hear a farmer condemn the system. I am not surprised when the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), or wherever the hell he comes from, condemns the system; he is liable to condemn anything.
