speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
I want hon. members to think about farmers and farm organizations; when they look at Hansard they expect to see a straightforward account of what this bill will mean to them. I hope they will derive more benefit from the last few speeches than they have derived from previous speeches. They look to this House for sharp, clear-cut, thought-provoking debate; they do not expect confusion.
Before I finish I want to set a few things straight for you, Mr. Speaker, and for the farmers of this nation. The bill calls for shortening the base period to five years. We did this because the ten-year period proved to be too long. Costs and prices can change so sharply in a ten-year period that the base price no longer does its job. And that is exactly what did happen. Right now the legislation on our statute books is little more than token legislation.
Let me refer to a comparison some hon. members have made. They say that all I have done is improve on old legislation. I ask them to think of what the Wright brothers did when they made the first successful powered flight at Kitty-hawk; then let them think of the sort of aircraft they fly home in, the DC-8 and Boeing 747. Certainly, these are airplanes, but they are big, magnificent improvements over the original. That is exactly what we are doing with this legislation; that is exactly the type of job we try to do in parliament. We do not tear down this institution and build it up again. We try to improve it all the time. That is exactly what we do on our farms. We improve livestock breeding, plant cultivation, horticulture, and our cultivation procedures. We try to improve all the time.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: Then bring in 29 more beef policies.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
That is exactly what we are trying to do with this legislation. I cannot understand all the criticism of this bill. Such criticism is not based on any philosophy.
Stabilization law must be more than just that. It is set up to be stop-loss legislation. However, to do its job the support price must be high enough to save efficient producers from going out of production when prices nose dive. There is nothing in this bill for those who are not productive. This legislation will not rob efficient producers of incentive, no matter what anyone says.
Many members have taken pokes at the five-year period. They say it is still too long. They would be right if the bill did not go any further; but it does, it goes a lot further. This bill builds an indexing system, and this index will be tied to everyday costs of production. This is our check on the five-year base. If the base lags behind changes in production costs, the index will make up the difference. The index will keep stabilization legislation current in the

March 14, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
same way as the cost of living index keeps a pensioner's cheque current. In the debate many members chose to overlook this index. Well, I will tell you one thing: if you overlook the index you are overlooking what farmers feel is the most important part of this bill. Farm organizations presented briefs to us in which they asked for this index. Think about that. What they want has been incorporated in this legislation.
Some hon. members of the opposition have charged that this bill has nothing new in it. If you want to know how off-base these charges are, ask a farmer. I will give you an example to prove my point. Say the bottom falls out of the price of farm produce X. The base price over the previous five years was $2, but the index shows the costs of production are $1 higher than during the base period. What does that mean to the farmer? It means that the supply price will be 90 per cent of $2, which is $1.80, plus $1 to keep stabilization in line with today's production costs. That totals $2.80 a unit. That is the minimum under the new bill. Under the law we now have the farmer would only be guaranteed $1.30 if the average price over the 10 years was $1.63.
On the farm there is a big difference between a floor price of $2.80 and a floor price of $1.30. Some members can say that is nothing. But farmers would again disagree. A price of $2.80 is 215 per cent of $1.30. Three factors lead to that 215 per cent increase. One is the five-year base period. The second is the index. The third is also important. The named commodities under this new bill cannot be supported at less than 90 per cent of the base price. That is up from 80 per cent. This 10 per cent increase has been belittled by many people as a petty change. In terms of cash in farmers' hands, it is far from petty. Some hon. members insist that the old legislation is able to cope with today's demands. That legislation went on the books in 1958. I have already explained that we need up-to-date legislation so that what we can do what must be done to meet the changing needs of society. The example I have just given you is proof that the legislation we already have is not good enough.
Some hon. members point out that the current act has no ceiling, so that we can shelve our new bill and merely raise support prices whenever we need them. There are two purposes to stabilization legislation. One is to give farmers a floor price that will protect them from ruin. If the floor price is high enough, the legislation also serves another purpose. It gives farmers the security they need to invest in land, buildings, equipment and stock. Farmers want a realistic support guarantee written into the law. Using the old bill would probably mean less cash in their hands. It would also definitely not give them as much security to invest in their farming futures. It would not give enough security if they want to borrow from a credit union or bank.
One of the criticisms hurled at this bill is that it balkan-izes the country. It allows top loading. In short, this means that provincial governments and/or producers can pay the cost of boosting the base price about 90 per cent. The federal support will not give advantage to producers in one province over another.
The charges of balkanizing could be true if the government of one province raised the base price to 95 per cent or

100 per cent of the five-year average, while the level stayed at 90 per cent in the province next door. This could give one province's producers a competitive advantage over producers in another province. That is why any top loading of a product sold across Canada will have to be uniform in all provinces.
Say two provincial governments wanted to pay the cost of increasing the base price for hogs to 100 per cent and the other eight provinces only wanted to increase it to 95 per cent. If the two provinces would not agree on 95 per cent, then the federal government would have no choice. It would have to withdraw all federal money form the stabilization of that commodity in those two provinces. That is wielding a big stick, but we will use it to prevent federal money from being used to give one province an undue advantage over another. I am sure the provinces will respect this power.
The only exception is where the legislation provides for regional supports. This only applies where there are distinctly different regional markets in Canada for one commodity. Potatoes are a good example. Potatoes raised in the Maritimes sell in one market. Potatoes grown in the west sell in another. Few potatoes cross from one market to the other. So a regional stabilization plan in potatoes would not pit one region's producers against another's. It could work very well. But none of these plans for support will work unless there is a production agreement and a market for the production. I am not going to spend taxpayers' money on production so large that it would come out of people's ears, or on production which cannot be sold. That would waste our production capacities and waste energy and resources.
Some of you have called for the support level to be changed every six months. Some want it changed every three. Whether you know it or not, that is not criticizing Bill C-50. It can be done. But think for a minute, and you will find that it makes a lot more sense for some commodities than it does for others. Grain crops come off once a year. Because they can be sold in orderly fashion throughout the year there is no need to shorten the stabilization period. Where a shorter period may do a good job is in seasonal crops. When you ask for stabilization price periods to be shortened, there is one over-riding fact you must be aware of, and that is that every time you change the support level you risk disrupting the normal marketing patterns.
There has been a lot of dispute about the list of named commodities. I want to explain this. Cattle, hogs, sheep, industrial milk and cream, corn and soybeans, plus oats and barley produced outside the Canadian Wheat Board area are automatically covered under the new bill. And there is a good reason for this. These commodities, plus the prairie grains covered by the western grain stabilization bill, add up to more than 88 per cent of the total value of Canada's farm production.
No commodity is excluded from protection. I think I should repeat that. No commodity is excluded from stabilization protection. Butter and cheese are no longer named commodities because they are now covered by the Canadian Dairy Commission Act. The CDC receives money for its
March 14, 1975

support programs from the agricultural commodities stabilization account. Therefore, it is simply good housekeeping to strike them from the list of named commodities.
Eggs have also been dropped as a named commodity because the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency has the power to manage supply. They talk about more power. I think they are going to be given it because they are meeting at the present time, and will be meeting again next week. If CEMA is well run there should be no need to use stabilization legislation. Yet, as I said, no commodity is excluded. Eggs could come under the bill. The governor in council can select any product for stabilization if it is needed. Bill C-19 already guarantees a floor price for wheat grown outside the Canadian Wheat Board area.
There is one important part of the bill that has been poked at by members of the opposition. Some obviously do not understand how the deficiency payment works. Say the support price is $45 per hundredweight. However, farmers only got an average weighted price of $43 that year from the marketplace. What deficiency payment will the farmer get? He will be paid $2 on every hundredweight he marketed during that bad year.
That $2 is a flat rate. That is what the farmer who sold his animal for $46 per hundredweight will get. It is also what the farmer who sold his animal for $40 will get. The reason behind this is important, and it needs to be understood. Producers should not rely on a deficiency payment to make up for sloppy marketing, even in bad times. The way this legislation is written, a farmer who sells his product wisely and gets the top price will come out ahead. The farmer who does not market his product as wisely will be paid less. This way it is always in the farmer's best interest to bargain well and market wisely.
I resent people saying that this government did not put the legislation that is now on the books to its full use. That is hogwash. Between 1958-59 and 1962-63, the government spent a total of $220 million in stabilization. That worked out to about $44 million each year. Then the Liberal government came in. Listen to this. From then until the end of the fiscal year 1974-75 we spent $l*/2 billion. That works out to about $133 million each year, so do not say we do not do anything. Just think what you did not do with that good legislation you passed in 1958.
It is simply not true to accuse this government of not making the best use of the stabilization legislation we have had. In 1974-75 alone $318 million will be paid out in stabilization cheques, and that does not include the consumer milk subsidy or the two-price wheat support price.
Recently this House gave second reading to Bill C-34, amending the Farm Credit Act. The aim of the credit bill is to make more low-interest mortgage credit available to young farmers. This stabilization legislation we have before us goes hand-in-hand with Bill C-34. There is no way that young men and women should be encouraged to buy a farm without the protection of this stabilization legislation.
These are two planks in this government's farm policy. They are both part of the legislative framework that farmers need in the future. It is most important we have that.
This new legislation will let us do a lot more in stabilization. That's the plain truth. Some hon. members have
Agricultural Stabilization Act
charged that this is not the truth. They point out that because the main estimates for stabilization payments in 1975-76 are less than we paid out in 1974-75, this new legislation is backward, is not progressive.
They are wrong. The fact is that the main estimates in the Blue Book are for known expenses only. These are expenses that can be accurately measured for the coming year. The Blue Book estimates are, in fact, a minimum. In each year since we have had stabilization legislation we have spent more money than we budgeted in the main estimates-yes, in every single year. When the bottom drops out of the market for a farm commodity we need to be able to act right then. If we were pinned to the estimates in the Blue Book, how could we possibly respond to farmers' needs? Answer me that. When we need more money than the main estimates provide, we get supplementary estimates. Our Stabilization Act needs this kind of flexibility. If anyone wants to read the annual report they will see this happened for the past ten years.
Some have implied that we paid our stabilization payments with money from hidden sources. How can they possibly say that? Supplementary estimates are voted on, and each member knows it. Every dollar and cent spent on stabilization is on the public record. It is dishonest for any member of the House to suggest anything to the contrary.
Let us look at the figures the hon. member for Windsor West attacked. He points out that we spent $301 million on stabilization in 1974-75 but that the main estimates for this year are only $261 million. Therefore he concludes that we would make less use of stabilization legislation than we have in the past. As I said, that is not true. Remember that the main budget for 1974-75 was only $129 Vi million. We ended up spending more than twice that.

speechtext:
I presume I may now address myself to the matters raised by Bill C-231. If I am out of order I will again defer, but since there seems to be general agreement that I can continue along these lines, I shall do so. I should like to cite the basis of tradition upon which the name of our national day rests and remind hon. members, if they need any reminder, that the day on which we celebrate our national day is July 1-I have celebrated this day in many countries of the world, I have always done so proudly, and I shall go on doing so.
In the opening phrases of the preamble of the act which brought our country into being, we find the following words:
Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to be federally united into one dominion-
So we find the words "Canada" and "Dominion" in the first three lines of that preamble. The suggestion in the bill before us today is that we eliminate one of those words and replace it by another. Madam Speaker, we are forgetting our history.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REPLACEMENT OF DOMINION DAY BY CANADA DAY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REPLACEMENT OF DOMINION DAY BY CANADA DAY
speechtext:
The Canadas, according to our history, were Upper and Lower Canada. We have now come to accept the Dominion of Canada as incorporating the Canadas, and, at that time in 1867, the colonies which had enjoyed responsible government for many years, indeed, the first responsible government on this continent-Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Those four jurisdictions came together in the Dominion of Canada. The BNA Act was, of course, proclaimed on July 1, 1867, having been submitted on March 19 of the same year. It is on July 1 that we celebrate this gathering together, this federal unity in one dominion under the Crown of Great Britain, etc. We have used this particular form, and all the symbolism related thereto, throughout our history. I do not believe we should cast this tradition aside in favour of a formula which reminds me a little of "Air Canada" and similar expressions, but not quite.
The hon. member's suggestion is "Canada Day". I submit that "Dominion Day", the title under which we presently celebrate our national festival to commemorate the coming together of those four original sections of our country, to which was subsequently added the other six
Holidays Act
and, later, the Northwest Territories, is still perfectly satisfactory.
The proposer of the bill claims that the word dominion engendered divisiveness. I submit that divisiveness in this particular instance is in the eye of the beholder. I do not see it. The word dominion is a respectable word, one that stands on its own feet. It has a very impressive heritage. I could probably quote from any dictionary, but the one I have chosen is the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary which I obtained from the Library. I would just remind the House that this particular word reaches us in its present form via the old French "dominion," from the medieval Latin "dominium", meaning "property", and also from "dominus" meaning "lord, master".
I think all of these are reputable concepts, bearing in mind that they are interpreted in a democratic way. When we speak of dominion we are not talking about the feudal times through which this particular word was developed, but are referring to its modern sense in which it is a respectable word that need cause no divisiveness and which should give us nothing but pride in retaining.
The first definition of dominion given by the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary is "The power or right of governing and controlling". I think that is a worthy concept, one of governance, the state of being governed. We have to be in our particular society. We would not be the dominion of Canada if we did not have the discipline within ourselves to be governed and to accept being governed. The second definition is "sovereign authority". There is nothing the matter with that. That, too, is a worthy concept and should be preserved within the symbolism of our festivals and our parliaments. The definition also includes "sovereignty, rule, control". I submit to the proposer of this bill that these are words that need cause no divisiveness; indeed, they should be given the respect necessary to live in a modern society, one organized in such a way as to accord respect to other people. For this reason the notion being put forward in this particular bill does not gain my support.
There is one other aspect regarding the change of this word that I should draw to the attention of the House. There was brief mention in the preamble to the act which brought our country into being, and of which we have just cause to be proud, that there was a union of the Canadas. In other words there were two Canadas, an Upper Canada and a Lower Canada, before Canada as we know it today came into being. We must remember that this is part of our history. By transposing words from, if you like, our colonial past into the modern sense, let us not provide symbols around which people can become divided and say, "Well, this applies only to the other part of Canada, one of the Canadas, not to this part of Canada". The one word that covers all of Canada, the umbrella under which we all live, is dominion. That is the word, the symbol, to which we submit voluntarily and gratefully, and it is the concept to which I adhere.
So, Madam Speaker, in view of the reputable family from which the word dominion comes and which I will not see denigrated in the manner I have just heard, and because there were two Canadas before there was a

March 14, 1975
Holidays Act
Canada, I suggest we stay with the word dominion and refuse to recognize the change put forward in Bill C-231. With those few remarks about the manner in which we describe our national festivals and holidays, Madam Speaker, I will take my seat.

Madam Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson):
That Bill C-231 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REPLACEMENT OF DOMINION DAY BY CANADA DAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to speak for a few brief moments on this bill which now seems to be subject to amendment in the House. I should like to make a few brief remarks in regard to Dominion Day, and I now understand it is up to us to decide whether or not the subject matter of the bill will be sent to a committee.
While dealing with the subject matter, my lack of knowledge of the other official language has made me rather curious. In the French translation of the bill the last line reads "under the name of 'Canada Day' ''.whereas in the French it is "fete du Canada". I had always been under the impression that "fete" meant holiday, and that "jour" is the literal translation of "day". However, this is a small point which may get ironed out in committee if the bill does in fact get to committee.
I am pleased it has been decided to refer only the subject matter to the committee, on the clear understanding that there is another bill somewhere in the works which is going to have something to say about Dominion Day. I understand the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) is planning to introduce such a bill later in the session. It is not unusual in our history to have bills concerning the first day of July. A rather interesting comment was made about it some time ago, on April 17, 1879, a date to which I will refer a little later in my remarks. If we examine Hansard for that date, the question at that time was a bill to bring about Dominion Day, and Mr. Holton said:
-as the hon. gentleman had appealed to him, he would say that Bills from the Senate were treated precisely like Bills originating in this House.
There was some question about dealing with those which originated in the Senate. This goes on to state:
They went through the same stages, and were also subject to rejection very frequently. There could be no objection, therefore, in point of form. He thought there was a great deal of force in the suggestion of the hon. the Minister of Justice, that this proposal rested on an entirely different footing from the proposal of the hon. member for King's (Mr. Domville).
Mr. Mills then replied:
-he did not exactly see what was intended to be accomplished by this Bill.
Later it is reported:
He did not think this House had the right to say to a man in the employment of another man that he was discharged from any obligation to work on a particular day. Dominion Day was, he believed, universally kept as a holiday, at least, it was in Western Canada, but it was not kept under the authority of any Act of Parliament.
[Mr. Munro (Esquimalt-Saanich).l
I just quoted that passage from Hansard to show that the tradition of Dominion Day in western Canada goes back considerably further than it does in eastern Canada, and it was always observed in western Canada under the name of Dominion Day. It is part of the heritage of western Canadians that the 1st day of July shall be considered as the day the Canadian provinces joined to become a country.
As we were speaking of holidays I thought I should dig out a list of all public statutory holidays in Canada which
is:
DOMINION OF CANADA-in accordance with the provisions of the Interpretation Act, the Bills of Exchange Act, the Public Service Terms and Conditions of Employment Regulations, the Victoria Day Act as amended, the Dominion Day Act, and the Remembrance Day Act, the holidays to be observed throughout Canada are as follows:

"(a) is the provinces of Canada. Sundays, New Year's Day, Good
Friday, Easter Monday, Victoria Day, Dominion Day, Labour Day,
Remembrance Day, Christmas Day.
I understand it was only the result of a misadventure in this House that we do not have a holiday called Heritage Day. While I am on my feet I might point out an injustice that is occurring in this country because of the failure of this parliament to pass a bill to establish Heritage Day.
A number of people working in Canada were sent back to work by parliament. Parliament forbade them to remain on strike and ordered them back to work, I believe about two years ago. These were the non-operating union railway workers. They were ordered back by Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, and part of the arbitration award by Mr. Hall was that these people would get the Heritage Day holiday. As parliament failed to establish Heritage Day, that part of the settlement is not being observed, and in fact these people are being cheated out of a rightful holiday which was agreed to in the settlement which put them back to work.
I suggest that instead of bringing in froth like this, now would be an appropriate time to do something for these people in order to fulfil the contract on the basis of which they went back to work. We would be doing something then instead of considering the subject matter of spurious bills like this. I strongly recommend that the government get in touch with the railway companies through the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), suggesting that the honourable thing would be to give these workers one extra day holiday this year and one more to make up for the one they lost last year.
According to the act of 1879, July 1 is the day it was decided we should celebrate Dominion Day. Whether this is right or not, this is the day on which we did become a dominion. If we want to have a Canada Day, an utter independence day, or a day of transition from our former status, proud though it may have been, we should take some other day than the 1st of July. July 1 is the day that Canada became a dominion with various provinces.
If we want a Canada Day there are other days that can be chosen. Perhaps when we move on to days of even more freedom we can adopt the date of the Treaty of Westminster, which made the basic change in the Commonwealth. Perhaps we should adopt the day that the Righ Hon. Sir Robert Borden prevailed upon our allies in World War I to

give Canada a separate seat at the peace negotiations. That marked a real step forward for Canada toward full fledged nationhood. Canada Day might well be chosen as the day of Vimy Ridge, April 17, which strangely enough is the same date from which I quoted from Hansard when they were discussing Canada Day, which was some 40 years before.
There are many other days we could usefully celebrate on which Canada has taken a step forward in its progress toward full nationhood. The 1st of July was intended to be celebrated for one reason, and that was the day on which Canada effectively became a dominion. I understand that this parliament sat on that day for the first time, and there were great celebrations in Ottawa.
They didn't sit until November.
Don't tell us you were there, Stanley.

I do not see any reason for having a great deal of discussion on the subject matter of this bill. The bill is short and requires little discussion, perhaps just enough to straighten out its terminology. It might be well to obtain the feeling of the people throughout the country. It may well be their wish to change this old established holiday. I am not, nor are the people of my riding, among those who seem to think all change is progress. Surely there are some things we do not wish changed.
There are some things worth preserving. I should like to see a stop put to this constant ferreting out of anything traditional in order that it can be changed to something new and modern, with the result that none of us will eventually know where we came from even the day before yesterday.
I see that there are others who wish to speak on this matter. Let me conclude by saying that if the subject matter of this bill is referred to the committee, I hope it will have full and wide discussion and that the feelings of the people will be considered in the most meaningful fashion possible. This matter is of considerable importance to many constituents in western Canada who have lived with Dominion Day on the record for 96 years. For 96 years they have celebrated the 1st of July as Dominion Day, and they may well wish to continue doing so.

Madam Speaker, we certainly have no objection to the passing of this motion that will send the subject matter of this bill to the appropriate standing committee. That will be at least some progress in that the matter would receive further discussion. As a matter of fact, if the amendment had not been moved and we were dealing with second reading of the bill we would have been prepared to vote for the motion sending the bill itself to the committee.
A moment ago when I interjected by suggesting that the first parliament of Canada did not meet on July 1, 1867, but not until November of that year, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) wanted to know if I was here then. I was not, but I was here in the mid 1940's when we passed the bill changing the name "Dominion Day" to "Canada Day". As I recall, the sponsor of the bill was an
Holidays Act
hon. member for Matapedia, a Mr. Cote, I believe. The bill passed through all stages in this House, and people began to think we were going to start calling July 1 Canada Day. What happened? You guessed it; there were some in the other place who did not like to make that kind of change. So the bill did not become law.
As I say, I hope the motion to refer the subject matter of the bill to the committee will pass so that there can be further discussion of it. I hope at some point at least that much consideration will be given to two or three other bills on the order paper having to do with holidays. I have one in my name which asks for a ninth and tenth general holiday under the Canada Labour Code, one in February and one in August. I refer to Bill C-249. I also hope that some day the subject matter of that bill might go to the appropriate committee. I think the bill in the name of the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) calling for a Sir John A. Macdonald Day might receive similar treatment, and that its subject matter might go to a committee. I hope, and I am encouraged in that hope by what has just been said by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) in respect of the proposal for a Heritage Day, that we might get a holiday in February. The hon. member for Victoria spoke strongly in favour of this, and expressed regret that there was a slip of some sort which prevented us from getting it through a few weeks ago.
I have to remind the hon. member that it was his colleague, the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher), who denied the consent which would have made it possible for the subject matter of that bill to have gone to the committee some time ago. So, because the hon. member for Palliser is not here today perhaps we could deal with that one also when we have Conservative support.
I was a little taken aback by the fine line of reasoning used by my friend from Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) who quoted from the British North America Act and suggested that Canada means just Upper and Lower Canada, Ontario and Quebec. The hon. member said that the name Canada applied to those two parts of this country.
It did then.

Yes, they were Canada. The point I want to make is that as a person from Manitoba I think I live in Canada, and I think my friend from British Columbia lives in Canada. If he will read the British North America Act a little further he will find it says that, unless it is otherwise expressed or implied, the name Canada shall be taken to mean Canada as constituted under this act, this act at that time providing for four provinces.

I rise on a point of order, Madam Speaker. I think in all fairness in respect of the record it should be made clear that I was talking about the Canadas as they were in the beginning. If we might paraphrase or use broad parlance, as it was in the beginning there were Canadas, and as I said, clearly this concept of Canada and the Dominion of Canada put an umbrella over the Canadas, the two provinces which then

March 14, 1975
Holidays Act
existed. I think my words were quite clear at that time, but I want to make them doubly clear.

Madam Speaker, I do not object to that interjection. It does not seem to me that the hon. member changed the situation at all. He said there were two Canadas and that the phrase "Dominion of Canada" became an umbrella over those two Canadas, and the other two provinces. The name "Canada" was enacted as applying not just to the two Canadas that were there in the beginning but to the entire country constituted by this act. I submit that the name "Canada" applies across the country. If the hon. member were asking for July 1 to be known as Dominion of Canada day that might fit his argument, but to say that we cannot call it Canada Day and must call it Dominion Day because it was on that day we became a dominion I think is like, to quote his phrase, having it as it was in the beginning.
Now we are a country from Newfoundland to Vancouver Island and I do not think it is a venial or mortal sin to call July 1 Canada Day. As I say, a bill to this effect passed through the House I think in the parliament between 1945 and 1949, Canada's 20th parliament, but was turned down in the other place, and of course that puts me more on the side of it than I was even before. I hope the motion to refer this subject matter to the committee will be agreed to and that we will soon do something about Heritage Day and the other holidays that have been proposed.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member who has just spoken made some comment to the effect that I should realize that the Conservative Party prevented his bill passing. The hon. gentleman sits a long way from me in the House, but my recollection on that day was that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) had intended to put forward a private member's bill which was receiving fair consideration around the House, but instead the Liberals presented a bill. At that time I thought the NDP said no to the Liberal's bill and that the Liberals said no to the NDP bill. I could be mistaken because I sit at one end of the House and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre sits at the other end.
On the point of order-

speechtext: The hon. member is aware that this is not a point of order but rather a point of debate.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member referred to something at a time when motions under Standing Order 43 were moved. It was not my bill but Bill C-208 of the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) which was before the House. When unanimous consent was asked for that bill to be referred to the committee, not only did the hon. member for Palliser say no but he also stood up and spoke against it and thus blocked it that day.
Madam Speaker, I simply want to say that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is absolutely right. I was speaking of the day when the two conflicting bills came in under Standing Order 43.

Madam Speaker, I rise this afternoon to speak about this particular motion as one who has a regard for words that have a ring to them, and words which seem to be leaving our vocabulary at an amazing rate and dropping out of our conversations and out of our life in a way which I think will leave us impoverished rather than enriched.
There are several of these words which have to do with the country and the way the people in this country see themselves and the country. One of them is dominion; one of them is realm; one of them is kingdom. All these expressions can be applied to this country of ours, and all of them have a fine ring to them which has been hallowed by tradition and which has a reference to the form of constitutional government we have. I contend that we add nothing whatsoever to our national life, to our patriotism or to our civic pride by eliminating or removing these words as references or in fact as titles of the land in which we live.
I do not think it is necessary to go back to the history of the reason why the word Dominion has been in the name of this country, but the source was of the highest if we can believe the story that has been told about the Father of Confederation who was struck by the line of scripture which refers to dominion from sea to sea. It was in that spirit that the word Canada was attached to the country. There was something higher, greater and above the mere earthly involvement.
It may be old fashioned, but I still think there is something to be said for the somewhat mystic approach to one's country, and if we ignore that, we lose. I know it is too late now even to talk about these things, but it seems to me that there was an advantage to being a British subject that is not found in being a citizen. Perhaps that is an argument for another debate and it is one that I will not develop now, but in the concept of being a subject there was a promise of regard, protection and provision, for that was the basis of a very ancient system of government that provided certain guarantees to every subject in the land.
The whole problem with the idea of being a citizen is that we find that citizens disagree, and the people who run the show tend to be the ones who are in power at the moment, whereas the older idea of a monarchy-because this country is still a monarchy-suggested that there were rights for all individuals and that it did not really matter who was in power at the time because there was a relationship between subject and monarch that could not be broken.
Now we find that in this country there is an increasing tendency to cease using all such fine sounding words as dominion, realm and kingdom, and I suggest that if we let them go, in a very short time we will be confronted with actions that will move us to the next stage along the way to a form of government that is not Canadian, that is foreign to Canada.
Our history has always been the history of a monarchy, whether it was through the French regime or through the continuation of the British regime.

The Canadian regime.
March 14, 1975

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Now it is imperial.

The hon. member across the way cannot ignore the history and the evolution of government in this country that has taken place from 1608 onwards. I suspect in a way that it has been considerably more rapid in the years of the British regime. Of course we moved along to that remarkable invention of responsible government which we borrowed from the Mother of Parliaments. We owe an enormous debt and great freedom to the parliamentary tradition which we have borrowed. We tamper with it at our risk.
I suggest also that there is something about the term "Dominion Day" that enriches this country, this domain- another word which is related very closely. Domain is a word that has dropped out of our current speech, as almost all these other words have.
It is still used in French.

We are left with nothing at all to refer to the type and kind of country we have. We have the name of the country, but I think we still need an indication of the kind of country we have.
I am proud of the traditions that have come to us. I think that our form of government is the best guarantee of democracy to be found anywhere in the world. I made that statement some years ago to a well known sociologist at the University of British Columbia, Lionel Tiger, who has written many books. I wrote to him in response to a talk that he had given on CBC, and he wrote back to me. He was critical about what I had to say about the monarchy at that time. I was reading his book called "The Imperial Animal" which he wrote in conjunction with Robin Fox, and as I looked through the book I discovered the statement that the best guarantee of democracy to be found in this world was in the constitutional monarchy. I realized that through the years he had come to my way of thinking.
There was a footnote to the statement, and I hurried to see if in the footnote he had given me credit for the original thought. Unfortunately, he had not, he credited some learned academic from the United States for the comment. But I still feel that I had planted the original thought in his mind.
I hope that in these few remarks this afternoon I have planted some thoughts that may be considered through the years. I urge the mover of this motion, and anyone else who thinks in terms of dropping the descriptive designation of this land of ours, to think again and realize that in that action there is a loss and nothing is presented to replace it.

Madam Speaker, I surely did not intend to take part in the debate this afternoon, but the comments of hon. members opposite prompt me to make a few short remarks. I would like to reassure them. I see that my colleague agrees when I say that I will speak briefly, but it could be dangerous.
Madam Speaker, I have never understood certain things stated by previous speakers. I have been sitting in the House now for over 11 years. I was a student at the Ottawa
Holidays Act
University for six years from 1953 to 1959. I used to come here, but I never did understand why each time a Frenchspeaking or an English-speaking member-

-independently of your country of origin. I say again that I could never understand exactly why people refuse to look forward to what unites us all here in the House, that is, the creation of true Canadianism through respect for the past. I share the views of my colleague who spoke before me when he spoke of respect for the past, but I would like to add that respect for the past must not stop us from creating what we have been elected to do, that is to create true Canadianism.
I have great respect for the French regime of Canada which was replaced by the British regime. I like to live under the British parliamentary system, and I say so openly. That system gave us a lot in this country. But what is wrong in having true Canadianism? Every small step that can be taken in this House toward that goal should receive the unanimous consent of the House. When one is abroad and Dominion Day approaches, if one says that one must go back to Canada because it is Dominion Day, it does not mean as much as if one said-and that does not mean a lack of respect for the past-that one is going back because there are great celebrations taking place on Canada Day.

I would like to know, Madam Speaker, why changing the name Dominion Day to Canada Day would show disrespect for our old institutions.
We must remember one thing, Madam Speaker, that Canada is one of the very few countries that has known Canadianism through evolution and not through revolution. A country that was under the Indians and Eskimos became a French colony and then a British colony. We have known, slowly, a great deal of independence. We have stopped going to the Privy Council in Great Britain for civil torts and criminal matters.
I participated in the debate with my colleagues on the Canadian flag. I see some members on the other side who are still here who said then, "No Canadian flag because it is going to divide". They said "This Canadian flag will divide the country forever," yet today, only ten years after, people in all parts of Canada are proud to fly the Canadian flag.
This is a Canadian debate, we are having evolution and are proud to use the word "Canada" as much as possible- one flag and one country and two official languages. All of us together will celebrate next July 1, our great day. I do not see why we should have that long a debate. Regardless of the country of your origin, you should be proud to use the word Canada as often as possible. I use it anywhere in the province of Quebec and I like to use it everywhere-in western Canada-with the same intonation.

-the Canadian experience, Constitution, flag, and Parliament, and I think it is fair and normal that we should have a holiday called "Canada day".
